changes.before:
• Resource. The noun an API exposes, addressed by a URL in REST - for example /orders/42.
  • Endpoint. One addressable operation on a resource, such as GET /orders/42.
  • HTTP method (verb). GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE - the standard vocabulary for what a request does to a resource. PATCH (changes only the fields included in the request, unlike PUT, which replaces the whole resource) is the one whose behaviour is least obvious from its name.
  • Safe method. A method whose intended semantics are read-only, such as GET. Logging/accounting side effects can occur. Caching depends on method, response directives, authorization and shared-cache rules.
  • Idempotent method. A method where doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not.
  • Status code. The three-digit number classifying a response's outcome: 2xx success, 4xx the caller's fault, 5xx the server's fault.
  • Versioning. A way to change an API's contract without breaking callers still using the old one, for example a /v2/ path prefix.
  • Pagination (offset vs cursor). Returning a large result in bounded pages, either by a numeric offset or by an opaque cursor pointing at the last item seen.
  • Error contract. The agreed structure of an error response: a machine-readable code, a human message, and whether retrying is likely to help.
  • REST. An API style built on resources, standard HTTP methods and status codes, usually carrying JSON.
  • gRPC. A binary RPC (remote procedure call - the caller invokes a function on another machine as if it were local) framework built on HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers, typically used between a company's own services.
  • Protocol Buffers (protobuf). A compact binary format with a defined schema, used by gRPC instead of JSON.
  • GraphQL. A query language letting the caller ask for exactly the fields it needs from a single endpoint, instead of one endpoint per resource.
  • Over-fetching / under-fetching. Getting more fields than needed, or needing several round trips to get enough fields - both common REST problems that GraphQL targets.
  • TCP. A connection-oriented transport that provides an ordered byte stream while communication succeeds, without guaranteeing application processing, at the cost of a handshake and of one lost packet blocking data queued behind it.
  • UDP. A connectionless transport that sends packets with no delivery or ordering guarantee, trading reliability for lower latency and overhead.
  • HTTP/2. The HTTP version that multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection, removing the need for many parallel connections.
  • Multiplexing. Running several logical streams over one shared connection at once.
  • Head-of-line blocking. One lost or slow item blocking everything queued behind it on the same channel, even though the items are otherwise unrelated.
  • WebSocket (Short polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets) - a protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent, full-duplex channel, so either side can send at any time without a new request.
  • Full-duplex. Both sides of a connection can send and receive at the same time.
  • API gateway. A single entry point that terminates client traffic and applies cross-cutting concerns - authentication, rate limiting, routing to the right backend service.
  • Load balancer. The component that spreads incoming connections or requests across healthy replicas of one service.
  • Round robin. A load-balancing algorithm that sends each new request to the next replica in a fixed rotation, which shares out requests evenly but not work, so a replica stuck on expensive requests still gets its full share of new ones.
  • Least connections. A load-balancing algorithm that sends a request to whichever replica currently has the fewest open connections.
  • Weighted. A variant of round robin or least connections where each replica gets a per-machine weight, so a bigger machine gets a proportionally larger share.
  • Consistent hashing (Consistent hashing: the ring, virtual nodes, and why it limits data movement) - a hashing scheme mapping requests and replicas onto a ring, so adding or removing one replica reshuffles only a small fraction of the keys.
  • Network layers. Network software is described as a stack of layers; the two named constantly here are layer 4, where a connection is only an address and a port, and layer 7, where the message itself is visible (see The network layers, all seven of them).
  • Layer 4 (L4) / Layer 7 (L7) load balancing. An L4 balancer picks a replica from the address and port alone, without reading the request; an L7 balancer reads the request and can route on path, header or hostname, and can terminate TLS.
  • Health check (readiness / liveness). A probe deciding whether a replica should receive traffic. A readiness check controls whether it gets traffic; a liveness check controls whether it gets restarted.
  • Retry. Sending a failed request again - safe only when the operation is idempotent or the caller can tell whether the first attempt already applied.
  • Timeout / deadline. A timeout is the longest a caller waits before giving up; a deadline is a timeout that travels with a request across every hop, so each hop knows exactly how much time is left.
  • Idempotency key. A value the caller attaches to a request so a retried request is recognised as the same request and never applied twice.
  • Exponential backoff. Waiting longer after each failed retry, typically doubling the wait each time.
  • Jitter. Random variation added to a backoff delay, so many clients that failed at the same moment do not all retry at the same instant.
  • Batching. Grouping several small units of work into one larger call to spread a fixed per-call cost across all of them, paid for by the wait the first item in the batch sits through.
  • Backpressure. A saturated component telling its callers to slow down or accept rejection, instead of accepting unbounded work.
  • Tail latency. The latency of the slowest fraction of requests, usually reported as p99 (the value below which 99 percent of measurements fall, so it is the slow tail rather than the average) or p999 (the same idea at the 99.9th percentile, an even narrower and slower slice) - see Requirements and capacity planning - which an average hides completely.
  • Hedged request. A second, duplicate request sent to a different replica after waiting a while for the first, using whichever answer returns first.
  • Load shedding. Deliberately rejecting or degrading some requests under overload so the rest still meet their target.

changes.before: A TTL is also a knob, not just a cleanup mechanism: shorter TTLs bound staleness more tightly and cost more origin load (more misses); longer TTLs cost less origin load and tolerate more staleness. Choosing a TTL is choosing a point on that trade-off for a specific piece of data, and it is worth being able to say, for any cached value, roughly how stale it is allowed to be before it matters.
changes.after: A TTL bounds time since cache fill when expired values are not served; it does not by itself bound age relative to the origin. With an authoritative, current refill and expiry enforced on every read, shorter TTLs reduce the possible stale interval after an origin change, at the cost of more misses. A lagging source, delayed refill, concurrent older refill or stale-while-revalidate policy needs its own source-age, version and stale-serving bounds. Choose the TTL and invalidation policy against that complete freshness contract.

changes.before:
Requirements and scale. A chat product serving millions of daily conversations, a first-token latency under a second, a bounded cost per conversation, and answers that are grounded in real sources and safe to show.

High-level design. A retrieval step - retrieval-augmented generation - fetches relevant chunks after enforcing the caller's source permissions, with the same authorization boundary on caches. A model router sends the assembled prompt to a policy-eligible model selected by measured quality, latency and cost, escalating to a stronger, pricier model only for a harder or lower-confidence request. The model streams tokens back to the user as they are generated. A guardrail layer checks the input for injection attempts or PII, and the output for policy violations and unsupported claims against the retrieved sources, before or as the answer is shown.

Hard parts. First, latency has two distinct numbers that both matter and call for different fixes: TTFT, measured across authorization, retrieval, queueing, prefill and first decode rather than assumed to be dominated by one stage, and TPOT, the steady per-token rate during generation - a design should name both rather than one blended "latency." Second, cost control at scale: every token in the prompt, including every retrieved chunk, and every generated token, is metered and billed, which is why chunk selection, prompt length, and a cheap-first router matter as much as raw model quality. Third, grounding and safety: retrieval supplies candidate evidence but does not constrain the model by itself. Citations must point to specific chunks, and a verification layer must check that each material claim is actually supported before release. If evidence is missing, the system removes or qualifies the claim, regenerates from supported material, or refuses to answer; deleting only the citation would leave the unsupported claim intact.

Trade-offs an interviewer will push on. Retrieving more relevant evidence can improve grounding, but insufficient evidence still requires qualification or abstention; extra chunks adds cost and latency and can dilute the prompt with irrelevant text. Routing aggressively to a cheap model saves money but risks quietly worse answers on hard requests, so the router's own accuracy needs monitoring, not just the model's. Streaming the answer improves perceived latency, since the user sees text immediately, but complicates a guardrail that would rather see the whole answer before releasing any of it - a later retraction cannot undo disclosure. If every material claim must be verified before exposure, buffer the answer for verification or release only independently verified segments.

Where machine learning fits. The entire product is built on a model, so the systems question is not where machine learning fits but how to keep it fast, affordable and safe at the traffic this product actually receives.

changes.before:
The cleanest control loop in ordinary software engineering is a Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler. It is worth walking through, because most backend engineers have already run one without ever calling it control.

The HPA measures CPU utilisation across the pods of a deployment, compares it with a target — say 60% — and adds or removes replicas to close the difference. Then it measures again. Put the names on it:

  • Plant — the running deployment.
  • State / measurement — current CPU utilisation and current replica count.
  • Setpoint — 60% CPU.
  • Control input / action — the replica count. The only thing the controller changes.
  • Disturbance — incoming traffic.
  • Feedback — measuring utilisation again after your own scaling action.
  • Controller — the HPA's scaling algorithm.
  • Damping — the scale-down stabilization window, which takes the highest desired-replica recommendation in a trailing window. It is not simply a fixed cooldown after the last scaling action; separate rate policies bound how quickly replicas change. Without it the loop flaps: scale up, CPU drops, scale down, CPU spikes, scale up.

Other software loops with the same anatomy: TCP congestion control (measurement is loss or delay, action is window size), a rate limiter whose refill rate adapts to a measured outcome, adaptive load shedding, and retry with exponential backoff and jitter — where the jitter exists precisely to stop many independent loops synchronising into an oscillation.

changes.before:
• A13. Choose relational by default when data has clear relationships, the application needs multi-row transactions, and query patterns are not fully known up front. Choose NoSQL when you need to scale writes horizontally beyond one primary, the access pattern is simple and known in advance, or the data does not fit a fixed schema well. Most large systems use both: a relational store for core transactional data and NoSQL stores for pieces that need to scale differently, such as a session store or a feed.
  • A14. A B-tree keeps keys sorted in a balanced tree where every leaf sits at the same depth, so lookup, insert or delete takes O(log n) comparisons - about 30 for a billion rows. Because keys are stored in sorted order, a range query finds the start with one O(log n) descent and reads sequentially forward instead of scanning the whole table. The cost falls on writes: every insert or delete may rebalance a page, and every index on a table is another structure updated on every write.
  • A15. Choose composite index order from the complete workload: equality prefixes, ranges, ordering, covering needs and write cost. Most-selective equality first is not a universal rule when both equality columns are constrained. Prefix-only queries and supported suffix or skip scans matter; compare actual engine/version EXPLAIN plans and observed cost.
  • A16. Isolation levels restrict particular concurrency anomalies. The SQL standard read uncommitted level permits dirty reads; read committed forbids them but permits other anomalies. PostgreSQL implements read uncommitted as read committed and its repeatable read prevents phantoms, unlike the standard minimum. Serializable protects equivalence to a serial execution, with engine-specific retry and concurrency costs.
  • A17. Pessimistic locking takes a lock before reading or writing a row, blocking other transactions until release - safe under heavy contention but limits concurrency and risks deadlock. Optimistic locking reads a version number with the row and only commits the write if that version has not changed, retrying if it has. Optimistic wins when conflicts are rare, since it avoids paying for locks almost never contended; pessimistic wins when conflicts are common, since retrying an optimistic write repeatedly wastes more work than waiting for a lock.
  • A18. The SQL standard gives minimum guarantees, while engines may provide stronger ones. Read uncommitted permits dirty reads in the standard, though PostgreSQL treats it as read committed. Read committed blocks dirty reads but permits non-repeatable reads and phantoms. Repeatable read blocks non-repeatable reads; the standard still permits phantoms and serialization anomalies, while PostgreSQL's repeatable-read implementation also prevents phantoms but can still raise or permit serialization anomalies. MySQL InnoDB defaults to repeatable read; next-key locking is relevant to locking reads and writes, not a blanket description of every ordinary read. Serializable is strongest: successful transactions appear to have run one at a time, at the cost of blocking, aborts, or retries.
